title: TweetTaglish: A Dataset for Investigating Tagalog-English Code-Switching
venue: Proceedings of the Thirteenth Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (LREC 2022)
problem_statement: Tagalog and Tagalog-English code-switching (Taglish) are under-represented in natural language processing research and practice, lacking large-scale annotated datasets, linguistic analysis, and standardized benchmarks for computational modeling and language distribution identification.
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Tagalog-English Code-Switching (Taglish), Social Media (Twitter), Low-Resource Languages
theoretical_framework: Sociolinguistic theories of code-switching, including Goulet's (1968) six CS motivations, Bautista's (2004) framework on communicative efficiency and proficiency/deficiency drivers, Hamers and Blanc's (2000) and Poplack's (1980) three-way CS typology (inter-sentential, extra-sentential, intra-sentential), and Flores's (2020) empirical identification of Tagalog-English linguistic markers (bound morphemes, enclitics).
methodology: Multilingual keyword harvesting on Twitter using six Tagalog CS-indicative linguistic features (magko-, di ba, talaga, ano yung, para sa, parang) across English and Filipino query settings to gather 21,150 tweets; preprocessing involving case normalization, stopword removal, and stripping of usernames, hashtags, emojis, punctuation, non-Roman text, and URLs; dictionary-based token-level language identification using PyEnchant for English, a scraped Tagalog lexicon, and rule-based morphological parsing for Tagalog verb conjugations; multi-label tweet-level language proportion assignment (percentages of English, Tagalog, and Other tokens); dataset validation via proof-of-concept regression modeling using 50-dimensional Filipino Word2Vec embeddings and six regressors (Mean baseline, OLS Linear, SVR, SGD, Bayesian Ridge, MLP) under an 80/20 train/test split.
datasets: TweetTaglish: 21,150 Tagalog-English code-switched and unilingual tweets collected from Twitter with word-level and tweet-level English, Tagalog, and Other language distribution annotations
Pretrained 50-dimensional Filipino Word2Vec embeddings trained on Philippine social media data (Marges, 2019)

inter_annotator_agreement.word_level: κ = 0.15 (slight agreement due to Spanish cognates and morphological blending)

key_findings: Constructed TweetTaglish, a novel dataset containing 21,150 Tagalog-English code-switched and unilingual tweets with token-level and tweet-level language distribution annotations.

Validated dataset learnability through regression benchmarking, where all models substantially outperformed the Mean baseline, and the MLP regressor achieved the highest performance (English: R² = 0.909, RMSE = 0.057; Tagalog: R² = 0.883, RMSE = 0.068; Other: R² = 0.797, RMSE = 0.068).
Observed that regression models predicted English language distributions most accurately, while encountering the greatest difficulty predicting the 'Other' category.
Determined the overall corpus language distribution per tweet to average 55.2% Tagalog, 19.4% English, and 24.5% Other.

N-gram frequency analysis computationally validated the efficacy of Flores (2020) Tagalog linguistic features for harvesting Taglish text at scale, revealing high frequencies of personal pronouns ('ko', 'ako') characteristic of informal social media discourse.

Validation of dictionary-based annotation against a human speaker yielded substantial agreement at the instance level (κ = 0.70), though word-level agreement was lower (κ = 0.15) due to cross-lingual cognates and affixation.
scope_and_delimitations: Restricted to Tagalog-English code-switched text gathered from Twitter without geographic or user-specific constraints.
Data collection relies on six specific linguistic query terms (magko-, di ba, talaga, ano yung, para sa, parang) rather than comprehensive lexicon search.
Empirical evaluation is delimited to tweet-level language proportion regression rather than token-level sequence labeling, dependency parsing, or code-switching point detection.
Feature representation is limited to static 50-dimensional Word2Vec embeddings rather than contextualized multilingual transformer architectures.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: One minor observation was that our current keyword search strategy allowed for the inclusion of text from some other non-English languages with similar phrases (e.g., Spanish, due to cognates such as para). This could be addressed in future iterations of data collection using more advanced regular expressions and text preprocessing techniques.
limitations.summary: The keyword search strategy and dictionary-based language identification introduced noise from cross-lingual cognates (particularly Spanish words like 'para' misidentified as Tagalog), contributing to low word-level inter-annotator agreement (κ = 0.15). Additionally, regression models exhibited lower accuracy on the 'Other' category containing slang, misspellings, and hybrid morphological combinations.

generalizability_gap: The dataset is limited to Twitter and Tagalog-English code-switching, leaving unaddressed other Philippine regional languages (e.g., Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon), formal or spoken discourse modalities, other social media platforms, and non-Tagalog code-switching pairs.
methodological_gap: Dictionary lookup paired with simple rule-based morphological parsing fails to robustly handle intra-word code-switching (Tagalog bound morphemes on English stems such as 'nakakatouch') and cross-lingual homographs/cognates; evaluations rely on static token-averaged 50-dimensional Word2Vec embeddings without comparing against contextualized multilingual language models.
future_work: Experiment with more advanced NLP approaches to effectively process code-switching in everyday text and learn better representations for low-resource languages, including Taglish.
Employ advanced regular expressions and text preprocessing techniques to filter out non-target language text and cross-lingual cognates during data collection.
Explore more complex downstream code-switching tasks, such as word-level language identification, syntactic/dependency parsing, and code-switching point detection.
